questions.problem: The work $W$ applied to a body is related to force $F$ and distance $d$ by the equation $W=F\cdot d.$ If $F$ is measured in Newtons $(\frac{\text{kg}\,\text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}})$ and $d$ is measured in meters, what is an appropriate measurement unit for work?
questions.worked_solution:
To find the unit of work, we substitute the given units of force and distance into the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =F\cdot d \\  & =\frac{\text{kg}\,\text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}\cdot \text{m} \\  & =\frac{\text{kg}\,{\text{m}}^{2}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the unit of work is $\frac{\text{kg}\,{\text{m}}^{2}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}.$

The force is measured in Newtons $(\frac{\text{kg}\,\text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}})$ and distance is measured in meters ($\text{m}$). Since the work is the multiplication of force by distance, we must multiply force units by distance units. Thus, we have

$$
\frac{\text{kg}\,\text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}\cdot \text{m}=\frac{\text{kg}\,{\text{m}}^{2}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}.

Thus, the unit of work is $\frac{\text{kg}\,{\text{m}}^{2}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}.$

questions.problem: The magnitude of a force $F$ applied to an object is related to the work $W$ and the distance $d$ by the formula $F=\frac{W}{d}.$  Given that $W$ is measured in $\frac{\text{kg}\,{\text{m}}^{2}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}$ and the distance is measured in meters, determine an appropriate measurement unit for the force.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the unit of the force, we substitute the given units of work and distance into the formula and simplify.

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =\frac{W}{d} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{\text{kg}\,{\text{m}}^{2}}{{\text{s}}^{2}})}{\text{m}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\text{m}}\cdot (\frac{\text{kg}\,{\text{m}}^{2}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}}{\text{m}\cdot {\text{s}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{kg}\cdot \cancel{\text{m}}\cdot \text{m}}{\cancel{\text{m}}\cdot {\text{s}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{kg}\,\text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the unit of the force is $\frac{\text{kg}\,\text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}.$

questions.problem: The gravitational force between two particles of mass ${m}_{1}$ and ${m}_{2}$ that are at a distance $r$ from each other is given by the formula ${F}_{\text{G}}=G\frac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{{r}^{2}},$ where $G$ is the gravitational constant measured in $\frac{{\text{m}}^{3}}{{\text{s}}^{2}\,\text{kg}},$ masses ${m}_{1}$ and ${m}_{2}$ are measured in kilograms, and the distance $r$ is measured in meters. Find an appropriate measurement unit for the gravitational force.
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the unit of gravitational force by substituting the given unit of the gravitational constant, mass, and distance into the formula and simplifying it.

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{\text{G}} & =G\frac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{{r}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{\text{m}}^{3}}{{\text{s}}^{2}\,\text{kg}}\cdot \frac{\text{kg}\cdot \text{kg}}{{\text{m}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{\text{m}}^{3}\,{\text{kg}}^{2}}{{\text{s}}^{2}\,\text{kg}\,{\text{m}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{m}\cdot \cancel{{\text{m}}^{2}}\,\text{kg}\cdot \cancel{\text{kg}}}{{\text{s}}^{2}\,\cancel{\text{kg}}\,\cancel{{\text{m}}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\text{kg}\,\text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the unit of the gravitational force is $\frac{\text{kg}\,\text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}.$

questions.problem:
A car dealership with $7$ sellers sells $50$ cars in a month. The owner uses the formula

$$
N=\frac{c}{s}
$$

to determine, on average, the number of cars sold by each seller, where $c$ is the total of cars sold, and $s$ is the total number of sellers.

Find an appropriate measurement unit for $N.$
questions.worked_solution:
We are solving for measurement units, so we can ignore the quantities $50$ and $7.$ They do not matter if we are just solving for units.

Since $c$ represents $\text{cars}$ and $s$ represents $\text{sellers},$ the appropriate measurement unit for $N=\frac{c}{s}$ is $\frac{\text{cars}}{\text{seller}}.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding Units When There Is No Cancellation
canonical_examples.problem:
The gravitational acceleration $g$ of a body in free fall is given by the formula

$$
g = \dfrac{2h}{t^2},
$$

 where $h$ is the distance, measured in meters, traveled by the body due to gravity in time $t,$ measured in seconds.
Determine an appropriate measurement unit for gravitational acceleration.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the unit of gravitational acceleration, we substitute the given units of distance and time into the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}g & =\frac{2h}{{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot \text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the appropriate unit is $\dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}^2}.$ Here, we ignore the unitless constant $2$ since it does not affect the units.

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding Units When There Is Cancellation
canonical_examples.problem:
The frequency of a wave is given by the formula

$$
f = \dfrac{v}{l},
$$

where $v$ represents the velocity of the wave in $\dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}},$ while $l$ represents the length of the wave in meters. Find an appropriate measurement unit for frequency.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can find the unit of frequency by substituting the given units of velocity and length into the formula and simplifying. 

$$
\begin{aligned}f & =\frac{v}{l} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}})}{\text{m}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\text{m}}\cdot (\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{m}}{\text{m}\cdot \text{s}} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{\text{m}}}{\cancel{\text{m}}\cdot \text{s}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\text{s}}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the unit of frequency is $\dfrac{1}{\textrm{s}}.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Dividing Nonstandard Units
canonical_examples.problem:
A farm with $115$ chickens produces $20\,000$ eggs per year.  To determine the number of eggs $P$ produced by one chicken on average, the farmer uses the formula

$$
P=\dfrac{N}{C},
$$

where $N$ is the number of eggs produced by the farm during the year, and $C$ is the number of chickens on the farm. 

In words, what is the appropriate measurement unit for $P?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We are solving for measurement units, so we can ignore the quantities $115$ and $20\,000.$ They do not matter if we are just solving for units.

Since $N$ represents $\textrm{eggs}$ and $C$ represents $\textrm{chickens},$ the appropriate measurement unit for $P=\dfrac{N}{C}$ is $\dfrac{\textrm{eggs}}{\textrm{chickens}}.$ In words, this is "eggs per chicken."

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The formula for the speed $S$ of a moving object is

$$
S=\dfrac{D}{T},
$$

where $D$ is the distance covered, and $T$ is the time taken.

For example, if a car travels a distance of $600\,\textrm{m}$ within a time of $30\,\textrm{s},$ at constant speed, then we can find the speed of the car using the formula as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =\frac{D}{T} \\  & =\frac{600}{30} \\  & =20\end{aligned}
$$

But what is the unit of speed? We can find it by substituting the units for distance and time into the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =\frac{D}{T} \\  & =\frac{\text{meters}}{\text{seconds}} \\  & =\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the speed of the car is $20\,\textrm{m}/\textrm{s}.$ When the unit has a quotient like this, we say "meters *per* second."

But what is the unit of speed? We can find it by substituting the units for distance and time into the formula:

tutorials.name: Formulas With Non-Standard Units
tutorials.problem:
Sometimes, we can be given a formula with values whose units are not the standard ones we know.

For instance, suppose the formula for a person's popularity $P$ is given by

$$
P=\dfrac{2f}{s},
$$

where $f$ is the number of friends that person has, and $s$ is the number of siblings they have.

If we want to find the unit of popularity, then we need to substitute the units for the number of friends ($f$) and the number of siblings ($s$) into the formula.

- The units for the number of friends is '$\textrm{friends}$' since we say 'I have $5$ friends'.

- Similarly, the units for the number of siblings is '$\textrm{siblings}.$'

Substituting these units into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =\frac{2f}{s} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot \text{friends}}{\text{siblings}} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\text{friends}}{\text{siblings}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the appropriate unit is $\dfrac{\textrm{friends}}{\textrm{siblings}}$, or "friends per sibling." Here we ignore the constant $2$ since it does not affect the units.
